solution: \(C=\{b, d\}\) and \(B=\{c, d, e, f\}\). Since \(b \notin B\), not every element of \(C\) lies in \(B\). So \(C \not\subseteq B\). The statement is False.
\(A=\{a, b, c, d, e\}\) and \(D=\{a, e\}\). Elements \(b, c, d\) of \(A\) are not in \(D\), so \(A \not\subseteq D\). The statement is False.
\(D=\{a, e\}\) and \(B=\{c, d, e, f\}\). Since \(a \notin B\), \(D \not\subseteq B\). The statement is False.
\(D=\{a, e\}\) and \(A=\{a, b, c, d, e\}\). Both \(a \in A\) and \(e \in A\), so every element of \(D\) is in \(A\). Hence \(D \subseteq A\). The statement is True.
\(B=\{c, d, e, f\}\) and \(A=\{a, b, c, d, e\}\). Since \(f \notin A\), \(B \not\subseteq A\). The statement is False.
\(C=\{b, d\}\) and \(A=\{a, b, c, d, e\}\). Both \(b \in A\) and \(d \in A\), so \(C \subseteq A\). The statement is True.

diagramNote: Rectangle U holding 1 to 20; one circle X containing 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14; all other numbers of U outside the circle.

solution: \(A=\{1, 3, 2, 7\}\). Any subset is formed by choosing some (or none, or all) of its elements. Three such subsets are \(\{1\}\), \(\{3, 2\}\) and \(\{1, 3, 2, 7\}\).

Every resident of Pune lives in Maharashtra and in India; every resident of Indore lives in Madhya Pradesh and in India; and residents of Maharashtra and of Madhya Pradesh live in India. So \(P \subseteq H\), \(P \subseteq B\), \(I \subseteq M\), \(I \subseteq B\), \(H \subseteq B\), \(M \subseteq B\).
\(B\) is the set of all residents in India, and every other set (Pune, Indore, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra) is a subset of it. So the universal set is set \(B\).

\(A\) (multiples of 5), \(B\) (multiples of 7) and \(C\) (multiples of 12) all consist of natural numbers. So the set of natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\) can be the universal set (the set of whole numbers or the set of integers would also serve).

\(P\) is the set of integers that are multiples of 4, which includes negative numbers like \(-4, -8, \ldots\), and \(T\) is the set of even square numbers. Since \(P\) contains negatives, the universal set must contain them too. So the set of integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) can be the universal set.

The universal set is all students of the class, and \(A\) is the students who secure 50% or more marks in Maths. Its complement \(A'\) is all the remaining students, i.e. the set of students who secure less than 50% marks in Maths.

Let \(T\) drink tea and \(C\) drink coffee. \(n(T)=80\), \(n(C)=60\), \(n(T \cap C)=20\). Then \(n(T \cup C)=80+60-20=120\). Students drinking neither \(=125-120=5\). Hence 5 students do not drink tea or coffee.

Let \(E\) pass in English and \(M\) in Mathematics. \(n(E)=50\), \(n(M)=60\), \(n(E \cap M)=40\). Students passing at least one subject \(=n(E \cup M)=50+60-40=70\). Hence 70 students passed in at least one subject.

Let \(R\) be rock climbing and \(S\) be sky watching, with total 220. \(n(R)=130\), \(n(S)=180\), \(n(R \cap S)=110\). Then \(n(R \cup S)=130+180-110=200\). Students with neither hobby \(=220-200=20\). Only rock climbing \(=n(R)-n(R \cap S)=130-110=20\). Only sky watching \(=n(S)-n(R \cap S)=180-110=70\). Hence 20 have no hobby, 20 do only rock climbing, and 70 do only sky watching.
_note: Book answer (neither 20, only rock 20, only sky 70) is CORRECT and internally consistent: 20 (only R) + 70 (only S) + 110 (both) + 20 (neither) = 220. The 'only rock climbing = neither = 20' is a genuine coincidence of the given numbers, not a transcription error.

solution: \(A \cup B\) is all elements inside either circle: the A-only, B-only and overlap regions. So \(A \cup B=\{x, y, z, m, n, p, q, r\}\).
The universal set \(U\) is every element in the rectangle: inside the circles \((x, y, z, m, n, p, r)\) and outside them \((q, s, t)\). So \(U=\{x, y, z, m, n, p, r, q, s, t\}\).
\(A'=U-A\), all elements not inside circle \(A\). With \(A=\{x, y, z, m, n\}\), \(A'=\{p, r, q, s, t\}\).
\(B'=U-B\), all elements not inside circle \(B\). With \(B=\{p, q, r, m, n\}\), \(B'=\{x, y, z, s, t\}\).
\((A \cup B)'=U-(A \cup B)\), the elements outside both circles. With \(A \cup B=\{x, y, z, m, n, p, q, r\}\), \((A \cup B)'=\{s, t\}\).
